pages.actualObservation: Title says Lecture Number 57, Demonstration on KUKA KR5 Industrial Robot. Footer 1.
Learning-outcome roadmap only: architecture, KRL, TCP/frames, RGB-D, ArUco, OpenCV, communication and pick-and-place. Footer 2.
Contents roadmap only, including SCHUNK gripper, D415, OpenShowVar, calibration, localization and transforms. Footer 3.

Architecture identifies six-axis manipulator, controller labelled KR C4, and smartPAD HMI. The numbered image distinguishes arm, controller, pendant and cabling. Controller functions include motion, I/O, diagnostics and safety. Treat generation/model descriptions as source-specific, not proof that every KR5 has identical hardware. Footer 4.

Cables carry communication and power between controller and manipulator. KSS is the robot software environment/interface; additional options include external axes, sensors, tools and technology packages. A software-function list is not a complete safety certification. Footer 5.

All five KSS responsibilities inspected: motion planning/interpolation/execution; digital/analogue/communication I/O; create/edit/execute/archive programs; variables/frames/calibration/configuration data; logs/errors/variable monitoring. Footer 6.

KRL proprietary language. Motion list PTP, LIN, CIRC, SPLINE; logic IF/THEN, SWITCH/CASE, FOR, WHILE, WAIT; I/O OUT/PULSE/SIGNAL/ANOUT; interrupts/triggers/errors/functions/subprograms. PTP drawing has a curved TCP path while LIN is straight; CIRC labels start, auxiliary and end points. These are instruction categories, not a complete executable program. Footer 7.

World global frame, Base workpiece frame, Tool end-effector frame, Axis joint-space representation. Image separately labels ROBROOT, WORLD, BASE and TOOL; robot root is not interchangeable with an arbitrary workpiece base. Calibration/accurate planning/repeatability motivations. Footer 8.

TCP is the effective tool point relative to flange. Four-point procedure uses the same physical reference under different tool orientations; it estimates position, not a complete orientation calibration. Exact wording needs measurement/conditioning qualification; repeated poses without independent orientation changes can be degenerate. Footer 9.

All eight steps read: select tool number, fixed pin/reference, record four differing orientations at the same point, calculate flange-relative XYZ, then verify deviations. This describes source procedure, not a command to operate hardware. Verification is distinct from assuming the fit is exact. Footer 10.

Photo layout identifies the fixed table reference pin near robot base and the mobile tool tip beneath the gripper fixture. Black circles and red label arrows inspected. They are separate points in the shown initial pose, coinciding only when brought together for a calibration observation. Footer 11.

Static PDF frame of TCP demonstration video labelled Random Start Position, Speed:4x. Viewed the actual frame only, not a temporal video. Playback multiplier is not an identified controller speed or physical velocity. Footer 12.

SCHUNK two-finger parallel gripper components: structural body and actuator housing, parallel jaws, pneumatic actuator, flange mounting interface, opening/closing air ports and contacting fingertips. No specific model ratings are given. Footer 13.

Double-acting pneumatic operation uses compressed air for both directions. Source-specific controller mapping is OUT[1] open and OUT[2] close; no complete valve circuit or interlock is supplied. Parallel motion does not by itself guarantee equal contact forces. Footer 14.

D415 RGB-D uses active stereovision with two infrared cameras, an infrared projector and RGB camera, streaming via USB. Depth and colour acquisition does not alone prove registered pixels; no numerical device specifications printed. Footer 15.

ArUco expansion is Augmented Reality University of Cordoba. Binary square fiducials carry dictionary IDs and support pose/reference estimation. A selected marker connects camera/robot frame estimates; dictionary identity alone does not supply metric pose or make duplicated printed markers unique. Footer 16.

Integration names Python, OpenCV, pyrealsense2, OpenShowVar, C3 Bridge and KRL. Camera processing estimates positions, communication transfers data, and the robot controller executes motion. No actual robot communication performed by author. Footer 17.

Checkerboard camera calibration across views estimates focal lengths, principal point, lens distortion and per-view extrinsic poses by reprojection fitting. Per-checkerboard extrinsics must not automatically be identified as the camera-to-robot transform. Footer 18.

Demonstration identifies KUKA KR5 Arc HW, D415 and SCHUNK pneumatic gripper; random coloured objects are localized in 3D, transformed and sorted. ArUco is the spatial reference and OpenShowVar communicates. This is a source report of hardware work, not an author reproduction. Footer 19.

System photo labels wrist gripper, marker board near base, external fixed camera on the right, work objects and cyan/magenta drop destinations. Destination-class labels need not match physical bin colours. The pictured board contains more than one marker; selected reference is safer than claiming only one physical marker exists. Footer 20.

Detection identifies marker corners/ID and uses PnP to estimate pose. Marker-frame coloured axes and sample object boxes/coordinates/confidence annotations inspected; coordinate conventions must be specified separately from the camera convention. A displayed confidence is not shown to be a calibrated probability. Footer 21.
Flowchart: RGB image, grayscale, corner/ID detection, rotation and translation vectors, marker coordinate frame. There is no executable code block. Footer 22.

Classical OpenCV colour detection explicitly avoids deep learning/trained models. HSV thresholds: cyan hue 87–128, purple 130–155, magenta 155–180, saturation/value at least 60. Inclusive hue 155 overlaps; ordinary 8-bit OpenCV hue is 0–179, so 180 can be an upper bound but is not an encoded pixel. Pipeline includes Gaussian blur, thresholding, opening/closing and contour-area gate 800–60000 pixels; implementation details are not supplied. Demonstration hardware validation mentions cyan/magenta. Footer 23.

Simplified flowchart goes RGB to HSV, colour masks, morphology, contours, centroid/bounding box and shape/position. A contour centroid is not generally its bounding-box centre; 2D centroids alone do not determine 3D positions. Footer 24.

Contour geometry supplies shape; image moments centroid plus registered depth and intrinsics give a camera-frame point, then robot transform. Six extracted outputs listed: colour, centroid, bounding box, shape, depth, pick coordinates. Depth-colour image has no numeric scale legend: colour alone is not a calibrated metric reading. Footer 25.

Component list distinguishes variable-access library OpenShowVar, communication gateway C3 Bridge, and controller-side robosync.src KRL synchronization/motion/status program. Neither the Python nor KRL implementation is printed. Footer 26.

Diagram orders Python/OpenCV, OpenShowVar, C3 Bridge, robosync.src, controller and robot. The text calls synchronization real-time but supplies no deadline, jitter or hard-real-time guarantee. Background-program language does not identify the exact KRL interpreter/task architecture. Footer 27.
Camera coordinates are mapped through a marker frame to robot base. A marker offset can be a general rigid pose; translation alone requires aligned axes. Footer 28.
Sequence separates camera-to-marker expression, marker-to-base compensation and tool/TCP motion. A perceived object point is not automatically a complete six-dimensional desired TCP pose. Footer 29.

Actual equation and seven-frame graph inspected: T_W_R T_R_F(theta1...theta6) T_F_TCP T_TCP_O = T_W_R T_R_M T_M_C T_C_O. Frame cancellation is consistent. PnP returns T_C_M, so T_M_C requires its inverse. The TCP/object relationship is not implicitly identity. Printed footer 30.
High-level sequence Home, Scan, Detect, Pick, Lift, Place, Return with distinct purposes. Diagram does not specify obstacle-free paths, all interlocks or numeric heights. Footer 31.

Pick stages current, safe height, object XY, approach height, grasp height, close, retract. Drop stages safe height, bin XY, place height, open, retract. Heights and world/base Z conventions are unspecified. Footer 32.

Integrated sensing: D415 RGB/depth, OpenCV detection, centroid/depth extraction, camera-frame point and ArUco reference. Calibration and alignment remain prerequisites, not supplied numerical code. Footer 33.

Transformed robot coordinates go through OpenShowVar/C3 Bridge to controller KRL and gripper execution, then home and next pick. No valid object after a few scans leads home; the numerical scan count is unspecified. Footer 34.

Two-column full pipeline inspected; camera/marker/image processing and coordinate transform precede communication/controller/program/robot/gripper stages. Serial conceptual depiction does not prove every runtime task executes synchronously or hard-real-time. Footer 35.

Actual static demonstration-video frame shows orange arm inside a cell, wrist gripper, coloured objects on supports, bins and external laptop. No time-resolved video or successful cycle count is available in this PDF frame. Footer 36.

Four error groups read: camera illumination/depth/distortion; marker size/placement/occlusion; robot TCP/mount/backlash; communication latency/synchronization/variable timing. Small errors propagate; systematic errors need not cancel. Footer 37.
Summary repeats architecture, KRL, TCP, RGB-D, calibration, ArUco, OpenCV, communication, transforms and full workflow; no new substantive claim. Footer 38.

Seven references inspected, including KSS8.3 manual, D415 and SCHUNK pages, C3 Bridge/OpenShowVar/py_openshowvar repositories and RoboDK. References are not evidence that hardware or omitted programs were executed here. Footer 39.
Closing thank-you page only. Footer 40.
